To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) second neoplasia is an emerging long-term complication of ASCT, 2) the risk of second neoplasias is higher in patients who received a BEAM or BEAM-like regimen, 3) the incidence of second cancer is 4.3 times higher than in the general population, and 4) the risk of developing second cancer is highest in patients who are older at the time of transplantation and in patients who received an allogeneic stem cell

the incidence of second malignancies after high-dose chemotherapy with autologoues stem cell transplantation for lymphoma is 16.8% (95% CI: 5.8-38.9%), and the age-adjusted incidence is 4.0 times higher than that for primary cancer in the normal population.
the cumulative risk of developing second malignancies is 16.6% (95% CI: 5.6-39.3) 13 years after ASCT, and that this risk is 4 times higher than the risk in the general population.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the incidence of second malignant neoplasms in patients treated with high dose chemotherapy and autologoues stem cell transplantation (HDT/ASCT) for lymphomas.
the development of second neoplasia following autologous stem-cell transplant for the treatment of lymphoma.
the incidence of second malignancy in patients treated with BEAC or BEAM for lymphoma followed up for a period of time of at least two years post-ASCT.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
second cancers following high dose chemotherapy with autogous stem cell transplantation are not rare and are not restricted to the first 5 years post-transplant.
ASCT recipients should be followed up for the rest of their lives.
second neoplasia after ASCT for lymphoma is a rare event.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the incidence of second malignancy after ASCT is higher than that of the primary malignancy in the general population and that the risk is increased in patients with a history of previous radiotherapy.
patients treated with high-dose chemotherapy followed by autologous stem-cell transplantation are at increased risk for developing second neoplasia.
the use of high dose chemotherapy and autologoues stem cell transplantation for lymphoma patients may increase the risk of second neoplasia, which is not a rare complication.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of high dose chemotherapy and autologouse stem cell transplantation (HDC/ASCT) in the treatment of malignant lymphomas is associated with the development of second malignancies, which adds significant morbidity, mortality, and costs to the procedure.
the incidence of second malignancies is increased after high dose therapy and autologous bone marrow transplantation (ABMT).
the risk for second malignancies is high in the long term and that it needs to be taken in account in the long term evaluation of strategies involving early intensification in lymphoma treatment.
